title: Gated Graph Neural Networks for Learning Hidden Independent Cascade Dynamics

paper.title: Gated Graph Neural Networks for Learning Hidden Independent Cascade Dynamics
paper.abstract: Abstract Information and infectious diseases spread through social networks, but the spreading probabilities driving them are hard to estimate without per-node activation times. Applications seldom supply these, and inference must instead proceed through indirect and noisy proxies for the terminal infection states. We study this inverse problem on a fixed, known graph under the Hidden Independent Cascade (HIC) model, with one spreading probability per node rather than a single global rate, so the number of unknowns scales with the number of nodes. Seed sets and observation parameters are known, while activation times and terminal infection states are latent, and the observed-data likelihood requires marginalizing over every spreading outcome. We propose a simulation-based amortized estimator that recovers the full node-level parameter vector without reconstructing individual latent cascades. Repeated seed-conditioned symptom observations are summarized as Symptom-Aware Cascade Features (SACF), which combine empirical symptom statistics with neighborhood and structural information. SACF are mapped to parameters by SAGE-HC, a permutation-equivariant gated graph neural network whose learned gates attenuate neighborhood messages corrupted by false positives and false negatives, and training on simulated HIC realizations yields a reusable inverse map. As a benchmark under the same hidden observations, we extend the Dynamic Message Passing learning framework to the HIC emission model. On synthetic and empirical graphs the two methods separate by topology. DMP is highly accurate on trees, whereas SAGE-HC is substantially better on heterogeneous, loopy graphs under noisy terminal symptoms.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Network models in general, and spreading dynamics on networks in particular, constitute a useful family of tools for modeling problems in epidemiology ( Pastor-Satorras et al., 2015 ) , finance ( Acemoglu et al., 2015 ) , information spreading ( Zapperi et al., 2025 ) , and many other fields ( Newman, 2018 ; Barrat et al., 2008 ) . Many widely used spreading models have only a small number of node states, discrete-time evolution, and simple local stochastic rules. One of the advantages of such models is their simplicity, which often permits direct computations and efficient Monte Carlo simulations. Nevertheless, inverse tasks for spreading processes, like recovering the parameters of the dynamics from observations, can remain computationally demanding, especially when the spreading process is only indirectly observed. In this work, we aim to estimate a separate spreading probability for every node from indirect observations made only after the cascade has terminated. The underlying dynamics follow the Independent Cascade model on a fixed and known directed graph, with one parameter per node shared across its outgoing edges, so the number of unknowns equals the number of nodes. The data record not the cascades themselves but what they emit, namely a known seed set and a noisy terminal symptom vector for each of a set of independent cascades. Neither the per-node activation times used by standard cascade-inference methods nor the terminal infection field is available. The parameters of the symptom-observation mechanism are assumed known, so the spreading parameters are the sole target of estimation. These two sources of information loss are of different kinds. The first is temporal. Observations arrive only after the cascade has terminated, so there is no ordering to induce the increasing sequence of activated subgraphs that standard cascade data provide. The second concerns the state itself. Because the terminal infection field is seen only through noisy symptoms, a positively symptomatic node need not be connected to the seeds through a path of live edges, and an infected node may produce no symptom at all. The observations therefore contain both false positives and false negatives. Direct likelihood evaluation requires marginalizing over a large number of latent spreading outcomes, separately for every cascade, and the resulting objective must be optimized over as many unknowns as there are nodes. In practice, complete cascade data can rarely be assumed. Our setting therefore arises naturally in applications where the underlying spreading state is latent and only noisy proxies are observed. Examples include financial markets, where private information diffusion is inferred from trading behavior or investor proximity ( Baltakys et al., 2019 ; Baltakys et al., 2023 ; Goel et al., 2025 ) ; epidemiology, where infections are latent and symptoms provide imperfect signals ( Braunstein and Ingrosso, 2016 ; Allen et al., 2020 ) ; cybersecurity, where alerts act as proxies for compromised systems ( Munoz-Gonzalez et al., 2017 ; Kazeminajafabadi and Imani, 2023 ) ; and online information diffusion, where latent adoption is observed through engagement or resharing behavior ( Bakshy et al., 2009 ; Taylor et al., 2013 ) . Early work on inverse problems for spreading processes focused on fully observable cascades and showed how maximum-likelihood methods can be used to learn model parameters or reconstruct the underlying network ( Saito et al., 2008 ; Gomez-Rodriguez et al., 2012 ; Pouget-Abadie and Horel, 2015 ) . In many applications, however, activation times are not recorded at all, and learning must rely on the final outcome of each cascade ( Amin et al., 2014 ) , where guarantees for recovering the network hold for tree-like graphs but weaken as short cycles become common. The observations may also be incomplete, with some nodes unobserved throughout, and they may themselves be noisy. Direct maximum-likelihood inference then becomes computationally expensive because it requires summation over the unobserved part of the system ( Lokhov, 2016 ) . One way to approximate this computation is to use Dynamic Message Passing (DMP) as a subroutine for learning ( Wilinski and Lokhov, 2021 ) . The resulting Scalable Learning of Independent Cascade Effective Representation framework was shown to handle several forms of noise and incompleteness in cascade data ( Wilinski and Lokhov, 2024 ) , and provides the natural likelihood-based comparison for learning spreading parameters from noisy and partially observed data. More generally, message passing is a widely used approximation for both forward and inverse inference in network dynamics ( Karrer and Newman, 2010 ; Altarelli et al., 2014 ; Li and Saad, 2021 ; Crotti and Braunstein, 2023 ) , including reconstruction tasks relevant to our work ( Braunstein et al., 2019 ) . Several other methods have addressed inference from incomplete cascade observations. In ( Dutta et al., 2018 ) , likelihood-free approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) is used to jointly infer a small set of spreading parameters and the source from multiple fully observed snapshots. Extending this line of work, Wang and Onnela (2024) used neural-network-compressed ABC to learn informative summary statistics and infer spreading parameters on a known network from a sequence of positive and negative tests, without observing infection and removal times. An autoregressive neural-network method within a Bayesian framework was proposed in ( Biazzo et al., 2022 ) , but its computational cost restricts its applicability to relatively small networks. Independent Cascade network inference from probabilistic terminal infection statuses was studied in ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , but focused on reconstructing unknown influence relationships rather than estimating node-level spreading parameters on a known graph. More recently, Manoharan et al. (2025) introduced the Hidden Independent Cascade (HIC) model and proposed a likelihood-free procedure in which a classifier is trained to distinguish observed cascades from simulated ones, while the model parameters are adjusted until the two become indistinguishable. Although effective for low-dimensional parameterizations, this approach does not scale effectively to the heterogeneous setting considered here, in which the number of unknown parameters grows with the number of nodes. We retain the HIC generative mechanism introduced in ( Manoharan et al., 2025 ) , but instantiate its spreading layer with a heterogeneous node parameterization. In contrast to the low-dimensional likelihood-free estimation considered there, our goal is to infer a separate spreading probability for every node from repeated observations of known seeds and noisy terminal symptoms. We address this problem using a graph-based estimator trained on simulated HIC realizations, which shares information across nodes through the graph rather than treating each parameter on its own. Our main contributions are as follows. First, we provide a formal mathematical formulation of the heterogeneous HIC inverse problem under noisy terminal observations, including the latent spreading process, observation mechanism, and observed-data likelihood. Second, we introduce Symptom-Aware Cascade Features (SACF) , which aggregate repeated hidden-cascade observations across cascades and seed configurations into structured node-level summaries. SACF combine symptom frequencies and variability with neighborhood co-activation, graph-distance, and self-seeded spreading information, without reconstructing individual latent cascades. Third, we propose the Symptom-Aware Gated Estimator for Hidden Cascades (SAGE-HC) , a permutation-equivariant graph neural network based on gated message passing. Training SAGE-HC on simulated spreading-parameter assignments and corresponding HIC observations yields a form of simulation-based amortized inference ( Zammit-Mangion et al., 2025 ) , learning a reusable inverse map from graph-aware cascade summaries to node-level spreading parameters. Fourth, we extend the Dynamic Message Passing learning framework of ( Wilinski and Lokhov, 2021 ; Wilinski and Lokhov, 2024 ) to the HIC observation model, providing a likelihood-based benchmark under the same hidden terminal observations. Finally, we systematically examine the effects of network topology, observation noise, training data, cascade budget, repeated feature realizations, and test-time observation budgets on estimation accuracy and stability.

sections.heading: 2 Model and Method
sections.text: Our approach consists of three stages. We first specify the HIC spreading and observation model, then construct SACF from the observed cascades, and finally use SAGE-HC to estimate the node-level spreading parameters.

2.2 Feature Engineering: Symptom-Aware Cascade Features
sections.text: Why not use the raw symptom observations? In the Hidden Independent Cascade model, the latent infection states 𝐙 ( m ) \mathbf{Z}^{(m)} are unobserved, and learning relies on terminal symptom vectors 𝐬 ( m ) \mathbf{s}^{(m)} . Raw per-cascade observations are highly variable: each cascade is a stochastic realization of the spreading process, while s u ( m ) s_{u}^{(m)} is a noisy proxy for Z u ( m ) Z_{u}^{(m)} . Thus, raw symptoms combine spreading variability with observation noise. We therefore aggregate observations across multiple cascades and seed configurations into Symptom-Aware Cascade Features (SACF) , yielding more stable node-level summaries that are informative about the underlying spreading parameters. Each coordinate of ϕ u \phi_{u} is constructed from the observed symptoms, seed sets, and network structure. These features are not intended to reconstruct the latent states Z u ( m ) Z_{u}^{(m)} of individual cascades, but to summarize observed spreading patterns that are informative about the node spreading parameter p u p_{u} . We instead generate multiple independent realizations per assignment using a moderate number of cascades, providing repeated stochastic views of the same target parameters while retaining both cascade-level variation and useful spreading information. The remaining task is to learn a mapping from these features and the graph topology to node susceptibilities. Since the information used to estimate p u p_{u} is contained in both the node-level summaries and the surrounding neighborhood patterns, we employ a graph-based learning architecture to capture these relational dependencies.

sections.heading: 2.4 Dynamic Message Passing
sections.text: We adapt a Dynamic Message Passing (DMP) framework for learning spreading parameters from partially observed Independent Cascade dynamics to the HIC setting, where only terminal noisy symptoms are observed. The resulting estimator is used as a likelihood-based baseline in our experiments. Details are provided in Appendix 5 .

sections.heading: 3 Results: Benchmarking with DMP
sections.text: We compare SAGE-HC with the HIC-adapted DMP baseline described above. Experiments are conducted on five graph topologies: a balanced tree, three Barabasi-Albert graphs with attachment parameters m = 2 , 3 , 4 m=2,3,4 , denoted BA(2), BA(3), and BA(4), and the Karate Club network. These graphs span different structural regimes, from an acyclic topology to increasingly heterogeneous and loopy networks. For each graph, we sample node-level spreading parameter vectors 𝐩 = ( p u ) u ∈ V \mathbf{p}=(p_{u})_{u\in V} and simulate HIC cascades to construct the corresponding 14-dimensional SACF representation. The benchmark uses 5,000 5{,}000 spreading parameter assignments, with 10 10 independent feature realizations per assignment and 50 50 cascades per seed. Every node is used as a seed. We consider two observation regimes: noise-free , with q = 1 q=1 and η + = η − = 0 \eta_{+}=\eta_{-}=0 , and hidden/noisy , with q = 0.6 q=0.6 and η + = η − = 0.2 \eta_{+}=\eta_{-}=0.2 . SAGE-HC is trained on pairs ( 𝐗 , 𝐩 ) (\mathbf{X},\mathbf{p}) and evaluated on spreading parameter assignments entirely unseen during training. The same held-out instances are used to evaluate DMP. Details of the assignment-aware split, feature normalization, and checkpoint selection are provided in Appendix 6.2 . We report Smooth L1 loss with β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 and Acc@0.1, defined as the fraction of predictions satisfying | p ^ u − p u ⋆ | < 0.1 |\hat{p}_{u}-p_{u}^{\star}|<0.1 . The balanced tree performs well in the noise-free setting but deteriorates substantially under observation noise, suggesting that its limited structural redundancy makes message passing more sensitive to corrupted terminal evidence. In loopy graphs, multiple paths and overlapping neighborhoods provide additional supporting information, which can help compensate for local observation noise. However, this benefit does not increase indefinitely: among the BA graphs, performance gradually degrades as connectivity increases from BA(2) to BA(4). Denser neighborhoods introduce more competing transmission paths and a larger amount of potentially noisy information to aggregate, making it harder to isolate the contribution of individual nodes. DMP shows the complementary pattern. Its approximation is particularly well suited to the acyclic structure of the tree, but becomes less accurate as the graph contains more alternative and dependent transmission paths. SAGE-HC benefits from some degree of structural redundancy, but excessive connectivity can also make node-level inference more ambiguous. Thus, the strongest SAGE-HC performance appears at an intermediate level of connectivity, where the graph provides sufficient redundant evidence without introducing excessive mixing of noisy neighborhood information. Since increasing the BA parameter changes both density and loop structure, we interpret this trend as an effect of overall connectivity rather than attributing it solely to loopiness.

sections.heading: Prediction Stability and Sensitivity Analysis.
sections.text: In addition to the benchmark comparison, we examine the stability of SAGE-HC with respect to the stochasticity of the observed cascades. For each unseen test assignment, the underlying spreading parameter vector is fixed while the model is evaluated on repeated feature realizations generated from independent cascade samples. Variation in the resulting predictions therefore reflects sensitivity to the particular cascade observations available at test time. Across all graph structures, prediction variability is higher under noisy observations, with the strongest increase observed for the balanced tree. This indicates that corrupted terminal symptoms make spreading parameter estimates more dependent on the specific cascade realization used for inference. Detailed stability measures and results are reported in Appendix 6.3 . We further study the sensitivity of SAGE-HC to the amount of training and observation data by varying the number of spreading parameter assignments, cascades per seed, graph size, and feature realizations used during training. Increasing the number of assignments and cascades produces the largest improvements in the low- to moderate-data regimes, after which performance shows clear diminishing returns. Repeated feature realizations also improve estimation, particularly under noisy observations, although the gains become small once the stochastic variability of an assignment is sufficiently represented. Across the graph sizes considered, estimation accuracy does not deteriorate as the number of node-level parameters increases. Finally, we examine whether a model trained under an observation-rich setting can generalize to substantially smaller cascade budgets at inference without retraining. Although performance decreases when only a few cascades are available, the model retains meaningful predictive accuracy even at strongly reduced test-time budgets. Performance improves rapidly as additional cascade evidence becomes available, with much of the gain achieved by moderate cascade counts and diminishing improvements thereafter. The effect of limited test-time information is stronger under noisy observations, although the gap between the two observation regimes narrows as the cascade budget increases. Complete results are provided in Appendix 6.4 .

sections.heading: 4 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied heterogeneous parameter inference for spreading processes when only the seeds and noisy terminal symptoms are observed, while the infection states and transmission paths remain latent. We first formulated the HIC model mathematically for this hidden-observation setting, including the latent spreading process, noisy observation mechanism, and observed-data likelihood. Building on this formulation, we introduced SACF, which summarizes repeated hidden-cascade observations into graph-aware node features, and SAGE-HC, a gated graph neural network that learns an amortized mapping from these observations to node-level spreading parameters without reconstructing individual latent cascades. We also adapted Dynamic Message Passing to the HIC observation model, providing a likelihood-based benchmark for the same inference problem. The experiments reveal a clear dependence on network structure and observation quality. DMP is particularly effective on the tree, whereas SAGE-HC performs better on heterogeneous, loopy networks, especially under noisy observations. The stability and sensitivity analyses further show that observation noise increases prediction variability, while additional parameter assignments, cascade evidence, and repeated feature realizations improve estimation with diminishing returns. A model trained with an observation-rich cascade budget also remains effective at substantially smaller test-time budgets. The present framework assumes a fixed known network and known observation parameters. Joint inference of spreading and observation parameters, transfer across related network structures, and applications where the latent spreading parameters are unavailable remain natural directions for future work.

sections.heading: 6.1 Synthetic data generation
sections.text: Training data are generated on a fixed graph G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) . Each assignment consists of a sampled spreading parameter vector 𝐩 = ( p u ) u ∈ V \mathbf{p}=(p_{u})_{u\in V} , which serves as the ground-truth spreading parameter. Conditional on 𝐩 \mathbf{p} , we simulate M M independent HIC cascades [ 20 ] and obtain symptom observations under the observation model Θ obs \Theta_{\mathrm{obs}} . The resulting observations 𝒟 \mathcal{D} are converted into SACF node features 𝐱 u = ϕ u ​ ( 𝒟 , G ) , u ∈ V , \mathbf{x}_{u}=\phi_{u}(\mathcal{D};G),\qquad u\in V, forming a supervised sample ( 𝐗 , 𝐩 ) (\mathbf{X},\mathbf{p}) , where 𝐗 = { 𝐱 u } u ∈ V \mathbf{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{u}\}_{u\in V} . For a fixed assignment 𝐩 \mathbf{p} , we may generate several feature realizations 𝐗 ( r ) ∼ P ( 𝐗 ∣ 𝐩 , G , Θ obs ) , r = 1 , … , R , \mathbf{X}^{(r)}\sim P(\mathbf{X}\mid\mathbf{p},G,\Theta_{\mathrm{obs}}),\qquad r=1,\ldots,R, by resimulating independent sets of M M cascades. These realizations share the same target 𝐩 \mathbf{p} but differ due to the stochasticity of the cascade and observation processes. This is important because SACF features computed from finitely many cascades are noisy empirical summaries of the latent spreading process. Including multiple realizations for the same assignment therefore trains the model to learn spreading parameter estimates that are stable with respect to finite-sample cascade variability, rather than estimates that depend on a single random cascade realization. Repeating this procedure over many independently sampled assignments gives the supervised training set. The observation parameters Θ obs \Theta_{\mathrm{obs}} are fixed and known in our experiments; hence, the learning task is to infer Θ diff \Theta_{\mathrm{diff}} , specifically, the node spreading parameter 𝐩 \mathbf{p} , from symptom-level observations.

sections.heading: Training protocol.
sections.text: Model parameters are optimized using Adam [ 24 ] with a learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} , weight decay of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and a batch size of 8 8 . The training objective is the Smooth L1 loss with parameter β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 ℓ ⁡ ( x , y ) = { 1 2 ​ ( x − y ) 2 β , if ​ | x − y | < β , | x − y | − 1 2 ​ β , otherwise. \ell(x,y)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}\frac{(x-y)^{2}}{\beta},&\text{if }|x-y|<\beta,\\[6.0pt] |x-y|-\frac{1}{2}\beta,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} Gradients are stabilized by clipping their ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm to 1.0 1.0 before each optimizer update. All models are trained for 100 100 epochs, and the checkpoint with the lowest validation selection loss is retained for evaluation. Input features are standardized independently by feature using z-score normalization. For each feature j j , the mean μ j \mu_{j} and standard deviation σ j \sigma_{j} are estimated exclusively from the training samples, and x ~ i ​ j = x i ​ j − μ j σ j \widetilde{x}_{ij}=\frac{x_{ij}-\mu_{j}}{\sigma_{j}} is applied unchanged to all training, validation, and test samples. Hence, the held-out validation and test assignments do not contribute to the normalization statistics. To ensure evaluation on genuinely unseen spreading parameter configurations, we use an assignment-aware hybrid split. Specifically, 80 % 80\% of the spreading parameter assignments are allocated to the development set, while 10 % 10\% and 10 % 10\% are held out as unseen-validation and unseen-test assignments, respectively. Within each development assignment, 10 % 10\% of the feature realizations are reserved for seen validation and the remaining realizations are used for training; no development realizations are used for testing. Checkpoint selection is based on the weighted validation criterion ℒ val = 0.8 ​ ℒ val , seen + 0.2 ​ ℒ val , unseen , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}=0.8\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val,seen}}+0.2\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val,unseen}}, thereby accounting for both within-assignment generalization and generalization to previously unseen spreading parameter assignments. Final performance is reported exclusively on the held-out unseen-test assignments. Each configuration is evaluated over five independent training runs.

sections.heading: 6.3 Empirical uncertainty estimation
sections.text: In addition to point-estimation performance, we examine the stability of SAGE-HC with respect to the stochasticity of the observed cascades. This is particularly relevant in the hidden-cascade setting, since the true node susceptibilities are unavailable in a real application and the accuracy of an estimated spreading parameter vector cannot be assessed directly. Repeated feature realizations provide a simple way to quantify how sensitive the inferred susceptibilities are to the finite cascade sample used to construct the input features. Recall that each assignment corresponds to a fixed latent spreading parameter vector 𝐩 \mathbf{p} , whereas its feature realizations are generated from independent sets of cascades under the same 𝐩 \mathbf{p} . Thus, variation in the predictions across realizations reflects variation induced by the observed cascade sample rather than a change in the underlying spreading parameter For a fixed unseen-test assignment a a , let p ^ a , i , j \hat{p}_{a,i,j} denote the predicted spreading parameter of node i i from feature realization j = 1 , … , n a j=1,\ldots,n_{a} . We first compute the mean prediction p ¯ a , i = 1 n a ​ ∑ j = 1 n a p ^ a , i , j \bar{p}_{a,i}=\frac{1}{n_{a}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{a}}\hat{p}_{a,i,j} and the corresponding sample standard deviation s a , i s_{a,i} across realizations. Following the standard normal-reference construction, we use p ¯ a , i ± 1.96 ​ s a , i n a \bar{p}_{a,i}\pm 1.96\frac{s_{a,i}}{\sqrt{n_{a}}} as an empirical prediction-stability interval, with the endpoints restricted to the admissible spreading parameter range [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . The resulting interval width for node i i under assignment a a is denoted by w a , i w_{a,i} . For each trained model, we summarize prediction stability by averaging the interval widths over all nodes and unseen-test assignments. We additionally report the corresponding mean prediction standard deviation, which directly measures the variation of the spreading parameter estimates across independent feature realizations. The procedure is repeated for each independent training run, and Table 2 reports the mean and standard deviation of the resulting run-level summaries. The intervals are used here as empirical measures of prediction stability, rather than as formally calibrated confidence intervals. A narrow interval indicates that the inferred spreading parameter remains similar when the same latent assignment is observed through independent cascade samples, whereas a wider interval indicates greater sensitivity to the particular cascade realization. Table 2 shows that observation noise consistently increases this variability. Both the mean interval width and the mean prediction standard deviation are larger in the noisy setting for every graph, indicating that spreading parameter estimation becomes more sensitive to the available cascade realization when the terminal observations are corrupted. The effect is most pronounced for the balanced tree. Its mean interval width increases from 0.0429 0.0429 in the noise-free setting to 0.1154 0.1154 under noisy observations, while the mean prediction standard deviation increases from 0.0346 0.0346 to 0.0931 0.0931 . This is also the graph for which the largest deterioration in point-estimation performance is observed under noise. A possible contributing factor is the limited structural redundancy of the tree. Message-passing GNNs construct node representations by aggregating information from neighboring nodes [ 16 , 19 ] ; in a tree, information between two nodes is transmitted along a unique path, whereas graphs containing cycles provide alternative routes through which related observations can contribute to the representation. Consequently, corrupted observations may have a stronger effect on the inferred susceptibilities in the tree. We interpret this explanation cautiously, since the present experiments do not isolate topology from the other factors affecting prediction difficulty. The BA graphs are more stable under the same observation noise. In particular, BA(2) and BA(3) yield the smallest noisy mean interval widths, 0.0576 0.0576 and 0.0582 0.0582 , respectively, while BA(4) and Karate Club lie between these graphs and the balanced tree. The results therefore suggest that the effect of observation noise depends not only on the level of corruption but also on the network structure through which the observed information is aggregated. In the simulated benchmark, the true susceptibilities are available and the stability measures can be interpreted together with the corresponding prediction errors. In an observed hidden-cascade system, however, the latent susceptibilities are unknown. The same stability calculation remains available because it depends only on repeated cascade observations and the resulting model predictions. It therefore provides a practical indication of whether the inferred spreading parameter vector is consistently recovered from independent realizations of the observed spreading process. sections.heading: 6.4 Sensitivity Analysis
sections.text: For the sensitivity analysis, we consider BA(2) graphs and vary one experimental factor at a time while keeping the remaining settings fixed. Unless stated otherwise, we use 5,000 spreading parameter assignments, 10 feature realizations per assignment, 50 cascades per seed, and 100 nodes. Results are reported for both noise-free observations and the noisy setting with p 1 = p 2 = 0.2 p_{1}=p_{2}=0.2 and q = 0.6 q=0.6 . We report Smooth L1 error and Acc@0.1 to access the performance. Number of assignments: Figure 1 examines the effect of the number of spreading parameter assignments while keeping the graph, number of feature realizations, and cascade budget fixed. Increasing the number of assignments consistently reduces Smooth L1 error and improves Acc@0.1 in both observation regimes. The largest gains occur between 10 and approximately 500 assignments, after which both metrics stabilize. This indicates a conventional learning-curve effect: additional assignments improve coverage of the latent spreading parameter space, but their marginal benefit decreases once this space is sufficiently represented. Similar saturation with increasing training-set size is commonly observed in neural-network scaling studies [ 32 ] . The effect is particularly pronounced under noisy observations. Acc@0.1 increases from approximately 0.73 0.73 with 10 assignments to approximately 0.92 0.92 once the number of assignments reaches 10 3 10^{3} , while Smooth L1 decreases from approximately 3.8 × 10 − 2 3.8\times 10^{-2} to 1.5 × 10 − 2 1.5\times 10^{-2} . In the noise-free setting, Acc@0.1 approaches 0.98 0.98 and Smooth L1 decreases to approximately 7 × 10 − 3 7\times 10^{-3} . Beyond roughly 500–1,000 assignments, further increases up to 10,000 produce only marginal changes. Figure 1 : Sensitivity of SAGE-HC to the number of spreading parameter assignments on BA(2), with the number of feature realizations and cascades per seed held fixed. Increasing the number of assignments substantially improves estimation at small and moderate sample sizes, after which both Smooth L1 error and Acc@0.1 approach a plateau. The noisy regime remains more challenging throughout. Error bars denote the standard deviation across repeated training runs. Number of cascades per seed: Figure 2 isolates the effect of the observation budget by varying the number of cascades generated per seed. Cascade count has a pronounced effect on estimation performance. Smooth L1 decreases monotonically as the number of cascades increases from 2 to 1,000, while Acc@0.1 rapidly approaches one. The largest improvement occurs in the low-to-moderate cascade regime, showing that a small number of cascades provides insufficiently stable evidence for accurate spreading parameter estimation. The effect is substantially stronger under noisy observations. With only two cascades per seed, Acc@0.1 is approximately 0.45 0.45 in the noisy setting, compared with approximately 0.68 0.68 in the noise-free setting. As the cascade budget increases, this gap progressively narrows. At approximately 200 cascades per seed, both regimes already achieve very high Acc@0.1, and at 500–1,000 cascades their accuracies are effectively saturated near one. Smooth L1 exhibits the same convergence, with both curves approaching very small errors at the largest cascade budgets. These results show that observation noise is strongly information-limited: additional spreading realizations can compensate for the reduced reliability of individual noisy cascades. This behavior is consistent with the broader sample-complexity literature on cascade-based inverse problems, where increasing the number of independent spreading observations improves recoverability and parameter identification [ 14 , 31 ] . Although these works address network-structure recovery rather than node-level spreading parameter regression, the underlying information-budget principle is closely related. The flattening of both curves at large cascade counts further demonstrates diminishing returns once the cascade-derived statistics are estimated with sufficient precision. Figure 2 : Sensitivity of SAGE-HC to the number of cascades per seed on BA(2), with the number of spreading parameter assignments and feature realizations held fixed. Increasing the cascade budget sharply reduces Smooth L1 error and improves Acc@0.1, with the largest gains occurring at low and moderate cascade counts. At sufficiently large cascade budgets, the noisy and noise-free regimes both approach saturation, showing that additional spreading evidence can substantially mitigate observation noise. Error bars denote the standard deviation across repeated training runs. Number of nodes: Figure 3 evaluates the behavior of SAGE-HC as the BA(2) graph size increases from 10 to 1,000 nodes. Performance does not deteriorate as the node-level prediction problem becomes larger. Instead, Smooth L1 decreases monotonically and Acc@0.1 increases over the tested graph sizes. The improvement is modest in the noise-free regime, where performance is already high for the smallest graph, but is considerably larger under noisy observations. The strongest improvement occurs between 10 and 100 nodes. In the noisy setting, Acc@0.1 increases from approximately 0.81 0.81 to 0.92 0.92 , while Smooth L1 decreases from approximately 2.9 × 10 − 2 2.9\times 10^{-2} to 1.5 × 10 − 2 1.5\times 10^{-2} . Performance continues to improve as the graph grows, but at a progressively smaller rate, reaching an Acc@0.1 of approximately 0.95 0.95 at 1,000 nodes. In the noise-free setting, Acc@0.1 increases from approximately 0.97 0.97 to 0.99 0.99 , while Smooth L1 falls below 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} at the largest graph size. Consequently, increasing the prediction dimensionality from 10 to 1,000 nodes does not lead to a loss of estimation accuracy within the investigated regime. The node-sensitivity experiment should, however, be interpreted as an end-to-end scaling experiment under a fixed per-seed observation budget, rather than as an isolated effect of graph size. Since all nodes are used as seeds, increasing the number of nodes also increases the total number of seed-conditioned cascade observations contributing to each feature realization. The observed improvement can therefore reflect both the richer relational structure of larger graphs and the greater aggregate amount of spreading evidence. Importantly, neither effect results in degradation as the number of node-level parameters increases. The progressively smaller gains beyond approximately 200–500 nodes indicate that the benefit of additional graph scale eventually exhibits diminishing returns. Figure 3 : Sensitivity of SAGE-HC to graph size on BA(2), with the number of spreading parameter assignments, feature realizations per assignment, and cascades per seed held fixed. Performance improves with increasing graph size, particularly under noisy observations, and exhibits diminishing returns for larger graphs. Since all nodes are used as seeds, the experiment measures end-to-end scaling under a fixed per-seed cascade budget rather than graph size under a fixed total observation budget. Error bars denote the standard deviation across repeated training runs where multiple runs are available. Effect of training-time feature realizations: To examine the role of repeated stochastic feature realizations, we vary the number of realizations available during training, F train ∈ { 2 , 5 , 10 , 20 , 50 , 70 , 100 } F_{\mathrm{train}}\in\{2,5,10,20,50,70,100\} , while fixing the strict unseen-test budget at F test = 2 F_{\mathrm{test}}=2 for every model. This controlled design ensures that all models are evaluated using the same amount of test-time information, so differences in performance can be attributed to the number of feature realizations used during training rather than to an increasing observation budget at inference. Figure 4 reports the results for 1,000 spreading parameter assignments. Increasing the training FPA from 2 to a modest number of repeated realizations improves predictive performance in both observation regimes. In the noise-free setting, Smooth L1 decreases from approximately 0.0051 0.0051 at F train = 2 F_{\mathrm{train}}=2 to about 0.0043 0.0043 by F train = 20 F_{\mathrm{train}}=20 . Under hidden/noisy observations, the improvement is more pronounced: Smooth L1 decreases from approximately 0.0101 0.0101 to around 0.0091 0.0091 , while Acc@0.1 increases from approximately 0.96 0.96 to about 0.970 0.970 . Beyond approximately 10–20 training realizations, both performance measures largely stabilize. Increasing F train F_{\mathrm{train}} further to 50, 70, or 100 yields only marginal additional gains. This behavior indicates that a small number of repeated realizations is sufficient to expose the model to the stochastic variability associated with a fixed spreading parameter assignment, whereas additional realizations become increasingly redundant once this variability has been adequately represented. The effect is more visible in the hidden/noisy regime, where repeated realizations are particularly useful for learning a mapping that is robust to observation corruption. Figure 4 : Effect of training-time feature replication on BA(2) with 1,000 spreading parameter assignments. The number of feature realizations used during training is varied, while the strict unseen-test budget is fixed at F test = 2 F_{\mathrm{test}}=2 for every model. Fixing the test budget isolates the effect of training-time replication from changes in the amount of information available at inference. Performance improves primarily for small to moderate training FPA, particularly under hidden/noisy observations, and shows diminishing returns thereafter. Error bars denote variability across independent training runs. Generalization across test-time observation budgets: We further evaluate whether an observation-rich model remains effective when less cascade evidence is available at inference. We use 5,000 spreading parameter assignments on BA(2), of which 4,500 are allocated to training and validation and the remaining 500 are held out for testing. Each assignment contains 10 feature realizations, and SAGE-HC is trained once with C train = 1000 C_{\mathrm{train}}=1000 cascades per seed. After checkpoint selection, the model is frozen and evaluated at C test ∈ { 5 , 10 , 50 , 100 , 500 , 700 , 1000 } C_{\mathrm{test}}\in\{5,10,50,100,500,700,1000\} . Figure 5 examines the robustness of a frozen SAGE-HC model to changes in the amount of cascade evidence available at test time. At inference time, the same held-out assignments are evaluated with progressively smaller observation budgets, ranging from 5 to 1,000 cascades per seed. Thus, unlike the preceding cascade-sensitivity experiment, the model is not retrained for each cascade budget; only the test-time observation budget is varied. Performance depends strongly and monotonically on the amount of test-time cascade evidence. In the noise-free setting, the prediction error decreases rapidly as C test C_{\mathrm{test}} increases, while Acc@0.1 rises from approximately 0.57 0.57 with only five cascades per seed to about 0.95 0.95 at 50 cascades and nearly 0.99 0.99 at 100 cascades. Further increases yield progressively smaller improvements, with accuracy approaching unity at the largest observation budgets. The hidden/noisy setting exhibits the same qualitative behavior but is more strongly affected when only a small number of cascades is available. Acc@0.1 is approximately 0.46 0.46 at five cascades per seed and 0.59 0.59 at 10 cascades, compared with approximately 0.57 0.57 and 0.70 0.70 , respectively, in the noise-free setting. The gap narrows substantially as additional observations become available: noisy Acc@0.1 reaches about 0.89 0.89 at 50 cascades and 0.96 0.96 at 100 cascades, and the two regimes are nearly indistinguishable at the largest cascade budgets. These results show that the learned inverse mapping transfers across substantially different test-time observation budgets without retraining. At very small cascade counts, estimation is information-limited because the cascade-derived representation is based on insufficient evidence, an effect that is amplified by hidden and corrupted observations. Once a moderate number of cascades is available, however, performance improves rapidly and then exhibits diminishing returns. The experiment therefore separates training-time data requirements from test-time evidence requirements and shows that a model trained under an observation-rich setting remains effective when substantially less cascade information is available at inference time. Figure 5 : Sensitivity to the number of cascades available at test time for a frozen SAGE-HC model on BA(2). The model is trained once with C train = 1000 C_{\mathrm{train}}=1000 cascades per seed. The same held-out test assignments are then evaluated using different test-time cascade budgets. The left panel reports prediction error and the right panel reports Acc@0.1. Performance improves rapidly as additional cascade evidence becomes available, particularly under hidden/noisy observations, and approaches a plateau at larger test-time budgets. Figure 6 : Comparison of accuracies at the 0.1 0.1 threshold of the noise-free and noisy training settings for a tree graph with progressively added edges to increase its loopiness Noise Robustness: We analyze how the loopiness of the graph influences the noise robustness of the model. To implement this, we start with a 100 100 -node tree graph and gradually add edges to increase loopiness. Figure 6 compares the accuracy at the 0.1 0.1 threshold of the models under the noise-free and noisy scenarios. The accuracy difference starts at 22.82 22.82 % for the original tree graph and gradually decreases with more edges added. For a graph with 4100 4100 edges added, the accuracy difference is just 6.11 6.11 % but the total accuracy is also lower, with the noise-free accuracy being 56.50 56.50 %. Both no-noise and noisy accuracies improve for the first 100-200 edges added and then decline steadily. This experiment indicates that the graph’s loopiness directly influences the robustness to noise of the model.
